A privilege is a special advantage, right, or benefit that belongs to a particular person or group — but not to everyone.

Think of it this way: if everyone gets something, it is a basic right. But if only some people get it, it is a privilege.

That exclusivity — the fact that not everyone has it — is the heart of the word.

Imagine a school canteen. All students wait in a long queue to buy lunch. But the class prefects get to skip the queue and go straight to the front.

Skipping the queue is a privilege — it is a special benefit given to only a select group (the prefects), not to every student.
The Two Broad Ways "Privilege" Is Used

1. Privilege as Something Formally Granted

Here, a privilege is an official, specific advantage that someone is given by an authority — a government, an institution, a company, or a rule. It is deliberate and usually documented.

  • A member of a club enjoys membership privileges — discounts, early access, or entry to restricted areas.
  • A lawyer and their client share attorney-client privilege — a legal rule that protects their private conversations from being revealed in court.
  • A diplomat enjoys diplomatic privilege — protection from being arrested or prosecuted in a foreign country.
  • A paid subscriber gets premium privileges — features that a free user simply does not have access to.

In all these cases, notice the pattern: someone in authority decided that a certain group gets a certain advantage that others do not.

This type of privilege can usually be granted and taken away. If you misbehave in a prison, you lose visiting privileges. If your membership expires, you lose your membership privileges.

2. Privilege as an Unearned Social Advantage

This is the broader, more modern use of the word — particularly in social, political, and cultural discussions.

Here, privilege refers to advantages that certain groups of people are born into or grow up with, simply because of who they are — their race, gender, wealth, religion, nationality, family background, physical ability, and so on. These advantages were not earned. They are not formally written in any rulebook. But they are very real in everyday life.

Examples:

  • A person born into a wealthy family may have access to better schools, better food, better healthcare, and better social connections — simply because of the family they were born into. That is class privilege (also called wealth privilege).
  • In many societies, men have historically faced fewer automatic barriers in workplaces, courts, and public life than women have. That set of automatic, background advantages is referred to as male privilege.
  • In a society where the majority group's culture, history, and appearance are treated as the "default" or "normal," members of that majority group move through life without facing certain obstacles that minority groups regularly face. This is called majority privilege (e.g., white privilege in societies where white people are the dominant racial group).
  • A person who was born without a physical disability can enter most buildings, use most transport, and navigate public spaces without a second thought. That effortless ease of movement is a form of able-bodied privilege.

The key insight in this use of the word is: having a privilege does not mean your life is easy or free of hardship. It simply means that that particular thing is not one of the obstacles working against you.

A wealthy person may still struggle with illness, heartbreak, and failure. But their wealth means that money is not an extra obstacle on top of all the others. That is the privilege.
Privilege vs. Right — What Is the Difference?

This distinction is important.

A right is something that everyone is entitled to, simply because they are a person. It is universal and should not be taken away.

A privilege is something that only some people have access to. It is not universal.

RightPrivilege
Who has it?EveryoneA specific person or group
Is it universal?YesNo
Can it be taken away?Ideally, noOften, yes

For example:

  • The right to a fair trial is (ideally) a right — every person deserves it.
  • A VIP seat at a concert is a privilege — only those who paid extra or were invited get it.
"It Is a Privilege" — The Polite, Grateful Use

You will often hear people say things like:

  • "It's a privilege to meet you."
  • "I consider it a privilege to serve this community."
  • "Going to university was a privilege I didn't take for granted."

Here, the word is being used to express genuine gratitude and humility. The speaker is acknowledging that what they have, or what they are experiencing, is not something everyone gets — and they feel fortunate for it. This is a warm, positive use of the word.
Privilege Can Be Visible or Invisible

One of the most important things to understand about privilege — especially the social kind — is that it is often invisible to the person who has it.

This is because privilege works by removing obstacles. When you do not face a certain obstacle, you often do not notice its absence. You just... move forward. But someone without that privilege hits a wall where you sailed through — and they feel it clearly.

A fish does not notice the water it swims in. A person with a privilege often does not notice the privilege, because it simply feels like "normal life." But someone without it notices the difference very clearly.

This is why talking about privilege can sometimes feel uncomfortable to those who have it — it requires them to notice something they have never had to think about before.

The word "privilege" is one that can be used casually ("VIP privileges"), legally ("attorney-client privilege"), or in deep social discussions ("white privilege"). But no matter the context, it always comes back to the same idea: an advantage that belongs to some, but not all.
